name: Neck bridges / wrestler bridges

lead: A neck bridge is an arch where the head or neck helps support the body, drawn from wrestling and grappling sports. Looksmaxxers borrow it to thicken the neck and get a stronger, more powerful look.

The position loads the neck and back muscles with bodyweight. It is documented in wrestling, judo and mixed martial arts, and general bridge references describe it as mainly for lower back and gluteal strength. No studies have tested it for neck thickness.

paras: People practise bridges as a bodyweight exercise, often borrowing progressions from wrestling training, as part of a routine aimed at neck size.
No injury data for cosmetic neck bridging were found, and risks are not documented in the available sources.

angle.text: Looksmaxxers borrow the wrestler's bridge from combat sports to load the neck with bodyweight and thicken it for a stronger, more masculine look. The exercise is documented in wrestling, judo and MMA, mainly for back and glute strength.

lead: A neck bridge, or wrestler's bridge, is a bodyweight position in which a person arches the body with weight carried on the feet and the head or neck. It comes from wrestling and grappling, where bridging is used to escape pins, and it is discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a way to thicken the neck. The appearance idea is that loading the neck muscles with bodyweight builds a bigger, stronger-looking neck that frames the jaw and balances the shoulders and upper body.

The general bridge exercise is described on Wikipedia as intended to improve lower-back and gluteal strength, and bridging appears in the list of techniques used in judo, Brazilian jiu-jitsu, mixed martial arts, wrestling and other martial arts.[1] The article covers hands-and-feet variations such as the bridge hold, bridge push-up and wall walking, and does not describe the head-supported wrestler's bridge or any safety guidance.[1]

In grappling terms, the bridge is an escape performed from the back: the pelvis is lifted so weight rests on the feet and the shoulders or head, often combined with a twist to dislodge or roll an opponent who is holding a dominant position; in Brazilian jiu-jitsu it is called an upa [2]. Strength-training forums borrow the neck-supported position, and some lifters on T Nation describe it as their main neck exercise [3]. Researchers have not examined it for neck size.
No study has tested neck bridges for cosmetic neck thickness.
infobox: Neck, upper back, spinal erectors, glutes, hamstrings
Escape from pins and mount positions [2]
Neck muscles that shape the neck
Sternocleidomastoid, trapezius, splenius capitis, levator scapulae [5][6]

paras: Bridge exercises arch the body so that only some points touch the ground. The common gymnastic bridge rests on hands and feet; the wrestler's bridge rests on the feet and the head or neck. Variations in the general bridge family include static holds, bridge push-ups, one-arm and one-leg versions, wall walking and closing from standing, which load the hamstrings, glutes and spinal erectors.[1]
In wrestling and other grappling sports bridging is used to escape pins, which is why the neck-supported version is associated with those sports.[1]
The bridge is described as an escape in grappling that wrestlers use to get out of pins, and it appears in wrestling, judo and Brazilian jiu-jitsu [2].
The neck-loaded version of the bridge appears in lifters' training logs as well as in combat sports, and it needs no equipment [3][4].

The sternocleidomastoid is one of the largest and most superficial neck muscles, running from the sternum and collarbone to the skull behind the ear. It rotates and flexes the head and is easy to see and feel on each side of the neck.[5] Deeper and posterior neck muscles, along with the trapezius, which shares its nerve supply, also contribute to neck width and to the line from head to shoulders.[5] These are the muscles that neck-training advocates aim to enlarge.

A broader anatomy reference describes the trapezius as producing the slope from neck to shoulder and the sternocleidomastoid as the most striking landmark on the side of the neck; splenius capitis, levator scapulae and the scalenes add to the back and side contours. The same source gives average neck circumference as about 38.7 cm in men and 33.3 cm in women and attributes the difference to greater muscle mass, body mass index and testosterone [6].

Neck bridges are mentioned alongside other neck exercises as an inexpensive way to train the neck without equipment. Looksmaxxing discussions about neck size generally pair training with eating enough to gain muscle.

On T Nation, one lifter wrote that bodyweight work suits the neck and that he had trained his almost only with wrestling bridges, calling it one of his stronger body parts [3]. A former fighter wrote that he had done many neck bridges and other neck work while competing [4], and another lifter listed front and rear neck bridges in a bodyweight routine [7].

These discussions sit next to weighted neck harnesses and banded neck extensions in the same training logs, and next to general advice to eat enough to build muscle. Looksmaxxing discussions of the neck describe a thicker neck as part of a more masculine, powerful-looking frame that balances the jaw and shoulders.

The general bridge article does not discuss the risks of neck-loaded bridging [1]. In forum logs, one lifter reported a neck strain after trying neck bridges at the end of a session [8], and another former fighter wrote that his wife no longer wanted him to do them [4]. No injury-rate data for cosmetic neck bridging have been published.

Neck strength itself has been studied for a different outcome: a study of 6,704 high-school athletes in 51 schools found that weaker neck strength and a smaller neck circumference were associated with concussion, with each additional pound of neck strength linked to 5 percent lower odds [9]. That study did not involve bridges and did not assess appearance.
No studies found. Medical literature on 'neck-bridge' devices concerns aneurysm treatment and is unrelated to the exercise.

lore.intro: Neck bridges come up on T Nation in training logs and equipment-free neck advice rather than in dedicated threads [3][4][7].
